tldr: Exact simulator gradients, which typically fail in contact-rich humanoid control, are stabilized through per-sample clipping and action-target regression, surpassing state-of-the-art world-model training efficiency on a single GPU.
overview:
Motion tracking—teaching humanoid robots to mimic diverse human movements—is attracting major attention as a foundational technology for whole-body control. However, prevailing zeroth-order (black-box) reinforcement learning methods like PPO treat the simulator as a black box, demanding huge sample counts and lengthy computation times. Meanwhile, first-order (gradient-based) methods that differentiate through simulator physics have notoriously failed within minutes on whole-body humanoid control due to sudden gradient explosions caused by stiff contacts.

Recently, methods using learned world models emerged to provide smooth "surrogate gradients," dramatically accelerating learning. But the authors realized: the real driver of this success isn't the world model itself, but simply the use of derivative information from dynamics. If rare unbounded gradient spikes and heavy computational costs can be addressed, the simulator's "exact gradients" should provide a far higher quality learning signal than any world model.

To prove this, the authors developed $\nabla$Mimic, a training method combining per-sample median-relative clipping with regression onto action targets, alongside NablaEngine, an ultra-fast GPU simulator that computes exact analytical derivatives of MuJoCo contact physics for the Unitree G1. Tracking all 40 motions in the LAFAN1 dataset with the Unitree G1, this method matched the score of the state-of-the-art world-model approach (which took 1.2 hours) in just 20 minutes, demonstrating remarkably stable learning on a single GPU.
contributions: Clarified the properties and trade-offs of exact simulator gradients versus world-model surrogate gradients in contact-rich robot control, both theoretically and empirically.
Proposed $\nabla$Mimic, which completely stabilizes exact-gradient training across thousands of parallel environments using per-sample median-relative clipping and action-target regression.
Open-sourced NablaEngine, a GPU simulator reproducing MuJoCo contact mechanics for the Unitree G1 that computes analytical adjoint derivatives matching float64 finite differences at ultra-high speed.
Achieved a state-of-the-art score of 0.82 on whole-body tracking across all 40 LAFAN1 clips with the Unitree G1 in just 20 minutes on a single GPU, without using a world model.

sections.heading: Why couldn't simulator gradients be used for humanoid control?
sections.summary: Humanoid motion tracking has been dominated by zeroth-order methods like PPO, which burn enormous samples and GPU hours. First-order methods differentiating through simulators failed due to contact-induced gradient explosions, but this work eliminates the root causes to unleash the true power of exact gradients.
sections.details:
Motion tracking—teaching robots to imitate human motion data—is indispensable not only for walking and agile movements, but also as a low-level policy for foundation models. However, the dominant algorithm for training these policies, PPO (Proximal Policy Optimization), relies purely on scalar reward feedback from the simulator, requiring hours or days of parallel GPU computation.

First-order reinforcement learning, which differentiates the physical simulator to directly compute how actions should change to increase rewards, ought to be far more efficient in theory. Yet in humanoid control involving stiff contacts with the ground and self-collisions, gradients explode astronomically at contact transitions. Consequently, even standard methods like SHAC diverge and stop within minutes.

Recently, SuperMimic avoided this issue by differentiating a learned world model, dramatically speeding up learning. However, the authors interpreted this not as proof of the superiority of world models, but rather as proof that derivative information itself makes learning orders of magnitude faster. A world model provides smooth, well-behaved surrogate gradients, but they carry bias because they differ from true physics. The authors started from the insight that by taming outliers in the simulator's exact gradients and slashing computation costs, exact gradients should yield even better learning than surrogate gradients.

sections.heading: A lineage of zeroth-order methods, differentiable simulation, and world models
sections.summary: This work sits at the intersection of four domains: reinforcement learning for motion tracking, policy learning via differentiable simulators, gradient utilization with world models, and highly efficient GPU simulator design.
sections.details:
### Zeroth-Order Motion Tracking
Physics-based imitation learning, pioneered by DeepMimic, has expanded to tracking thousands of clips with a single policy (PHC) and deployments on real humanoids like the Unitree G1. However, these rely entirely on zeroth-order methods like PPO. Recent large-scale studies required vast computational budgets, such as running 128 GPUs for 7 days to train on hundreds of hours of motion.

### First-Order Learning via Differentiable Simulators
Backpropagation through time (BPTT) across simulators has long been plagued by gradient explosions. To counter this, approaches like SHAC (combining short time horizons with TD($\lambda$) critics) or artificial contact smoothing via spring-dampers have been explored. However, these were limited to simplified contact models or small scales (dozens to hundreds of parallel environments). None succeeded on whole-body humanoid control across thousands of parallel environments with realistic contact dynamics.

### Learned Model Gradients vs. Simulator Gradients
Approaches like Dreamer and SuperMimic differentiate learned neural network dynamics, providing stability because gradients remain smooth and bounded. But this merely differentiates an approximation, not the simulator itself. This work chose instead to directly utilize the exact derivatives of the simulator itself.

### Differentiable GPU Simulators
While differentiable GPU simulators like Warp, MJX, and Genesis are growing, engines capable of computing full analytic derivatives of contact mechanics quickly and accurately in backward mode have been extremely rare. This study broke through the computational bottleneck by developing NablaEngine, a deterministic GPU simulator hyper-optimized specifically for the Unitree G1.

sections.heading: Task setup and formulation of first-order policy learning
sections.summary: The target robot is the 29-DoF Unitree G1 performing whole-body motion tracking at 50 Hz. Policies are optimized using pathwise gradients that backpropagate horizon returns directly through the dynamics.
sections.details:
### Task Setup
The target task is whole-body motion tracking for the Unitree G1 with 29 actuated joints. Control runs at 50 Hz (20 ms), and simulator physics steps 4 sub-steps at 5 ms each. Inputs to the policy network consist of noisy proprioceptive history over the past 10 frames (joint positions/velocities, angular velocity, gravity vector, previous actions), reference motion information across the next 10 frames, and the relative pose between the reference and current torso. The design eliminates the need for global state estimation.

### Reward Design and Termination Conditions
The reward function follows prior work (BeyondMimic and SuperMimic), combining exponential kernels for position, orientation, and velocity across 14 body keypoints, alongside penalties on action rates and joint limit violations. An episode terminates immediately if the torso height error exceeds 0.25 m or the torso tilt error exceeds a threshold (0.8), indicating a fall.

### First-Order Policy Learning Formulation
Over a window of length $H$ starting from state $s_0$, the return $J$ is the sum of intermediate rewards bootstrapped with a final-step value function $V_\phi$. If the dynamics $f$ are differentiable, BPTT can directly compute the policy gradient $\nabla_\theta J$ with respect to policy parameters $\theta$. Unlike likelihood-ratio gradients in PPO, this is a pathwise gradient multiplying dynamics Jacobians, meaning gradient quality is directly governed by dynamics characteristics.

sections.heading: Exact vs. surrogate gradients: Why the former broke and the latter worked
sections.summary: Comparing exact simulator gradients with world-model surrogate gradients reveals that while both align for the vast majority of steps, exact gradients contain rare, astronomical spikes at contact boundaries—the true culprit behind the divergence of prior methods like SHAC.
sections.details:
### Two Gradient Types and Their Trade-offs
Policy gradients containing the simulator's true analytic derivatives are called exact gradients, while gradients obtained by differentiating a separate system like a learned world model are called surrogate gradients. Surrogate gradients pass through Lipschitz-continuous neural networks, ensuring they remain bounded and cheap to compute, but they carry bias since they reflect an approximation. Exact gradients have no model bias, but they suffer from singularities where values diverge toward infinity at discrete contact switches, alongside heavy computational costs.

### Mostly Identical, Differing Only in Extreme Tails
Comparing both gradients along identical trajectories revealed an intriguing fact: across the vast majority of gradient samples (low-norm regions), their directions align almost perfectly with cosine similarities of 0.96 to 0.98. However, in the top 0.1% of extreme cases, exact gradients spike by astronomical factors of $10^8$ to $10^{24}$, whereas the world model smoothly compresses them. The key advantage of a world model was never low bias, but its ability to forcefully suppress extreme outliers.

### Why Standard SHAC Exploded
Conventional first-order SHAC uses global norm clipping across the entire batch. However, if even a single sample out of 4,096 parallel environments hits a $10^{10}\times$ gradient spike at a contact boundary, the entire batch norm explodes. As a result, global clipping either crushes the useful learning signals of the other 4,095 normal samples down to near zero, or triggers a gradient explosion guard that halts training entirely. Indeed, when running SHAC, every single seed terminated within minutes (0.06 hours).

### Horizon Trade-offs
Lengthening the time horizon $H$ allows gradients to reach distant rewards, reducing reliance on a biased critic. However, as the product of Jacobians grows longer, the extreme tails of the gradient distribution widen rapidly. Thus, choosing the window length is critical to performance.

sections.heading: ∇Mimic: Taming outliers and unlocking exact gradients
sections.summary: ∇Mimic safely and efficiently exploits exact gradients using two core pillars: per-sample median-relative clipping applied at every step of BPTT, and multistep regression onto gradient-derived action targets.
sections.details:
### 5.1 Per-Sample Median-Relative Clipping
To handle extreme gradients that distort batch-wide averages, $\nabla$Mimic clips the action cotangent (gradient) of each parallel environment at each step relative to $\kappa$ times the batch median (using $\kappa=10$ in experiments). The median is chosen because even if a single sample diverges to infinity, the median remains rock-solid. This reliably suppresses anomalous spikes while preserving intact the learning signals of the remaining 80–90% well-behaved samples. In ablation experiments, removing this clipping caused 1 of 3 seeds to diverge instantly, with the others suffering severe score drops.

### 5.2 Multistep Regression onto Gradient-Derived Action Targets
Evaluating exact simulator gradients is computationally demanding. To extract maximal value from each simulated window, $\nabla$Mimic adopts the PODS concept, using clipped gradients to construct action-space targets: $y_t = a_t + \delta \cdot g_t / \mathrm{RMS}(g)$, where $\delta$ is a physical update step size in radians. The policy network is then trained toward these targets using a separate Adam optimizer over $M$ steps of minibatch regression. This yields stable, substantial policy improvements without extra simulation steps. Replacing this with a simple single-step gradient update dropped the score visibly from 0.855 to 0.806.

### 5.3 Synergistic Safety: Bounded Action Targets
Combining these two mechanisms forms an elegant safeguard. Mathematically, the change in the target for sample $i$ is strictly bounded within $\sqrt{2}\kappa\delta$ (around 0.13 radians under default parameters). Without clipping, a single outlier sample could consume the entire update budget (roughly 15 radians), zeroing out updates for all other samples. Together, they ensure that every sample makes steady progress within physically reasonable bounds, regardless of raw gradient magnitudes.

### 5.4 Horizon Length and Residual Actions
A time horizon of $H=64$ proved optimal. Shortening it to $H=32$ caused performance to drop as critic bias errors dominated. Additionally, having the policy network predict residual actions relative to the reference motion (rather than absolute joint targets) allowed the robot to track the reference pose from the start of training, boosting learning speed and lifting the final score to 0.874.

sections.heading: NablaEngine: Solving full MuJoCo contact dynamics in a single GPU megakernel
sections.summary: Tailored specifically for the Unitree G1, NablaEngine tightly fuses MuJoCo's full contact dynamics and its analytical adjoint. The backward pass executes inside a single megakernel, outputting exact gradients for an added cost of just 0.57 ms.
sections.details:
### One World per Warp and the Megakernel Design
To maximize differentiable simulation speed, NablaEngine is custom-built for the Unitree G1 (29 DoF, 502 contact pairs). Each simulation world is assigned to a single GPU warp (32 threads), keeping all state variables in shared memory and registers. Forward simulation runs via two fused kernels per sub-step, while the backward pass (adjoint) across an entire 20 ms control step (4 sub-steps) runs as a single megakernel. Replaying all sub-steps in reverse without exiting the kernel eliminates global memory access overheads.

### Hand-Derived Analytical Adjoints
The backward pass analytically differentiates every stage: forward kinematics, collision detection, constraint force solving, and integration. In particular, for the Linear Complementarity Problem (LCP) constraint solver, rather than autodiffing solver iterations, it applies the implicit function theorem to the optimality conditions (equivalent to KKT conditions). By recording a tiny tape during forward execution (23.6 kB per world), it backpropagates through fixed active contact sets in one go. The result matches float64 finite differences from C MuJoCo with an ultra-low relative error of $10^{-5}$, while forward execution remains bit-level deterministic.

### Handling Geometric Singularities
Geometric derivative singularities occur in two scenarios: self-contact between feet approaching zero separation, and capsules crossing in parallel. NablaEngine introduces a safeguard that freezes (zeros) geometric gradient variations only when distances drop below 1 mm or angles fall below 2 degrees. Outside these tiny thresholds, the simulator's true exact derivatives flow unimpeded.

### Blazing Speed
On an RTX PRO 6000, 4,096 parallel forward steps finish in 1.21 ms. The full step including gradient computation takes only 1.78 ms. In other words, backpropagating through the entire contact dynamics and constraint solver takes just 0.57 ms—less than half the forward pass time. This is $11.5\times$ faster than the MuJoCo Warp adjoint implementation, simulating and differentiating roughly 18.8 hours of robot motion per wall-clock second.

sections.heading: Experimental results: Slashing 1.2 hours to 20 minutes, blowing past PPO and baselines
sections.summary: In experiments across all 40 LAFAN1 clips, $\nabla$Mimic reached the 0.82 score of the state-of-the-art world-model approach (SuperMimic, 1.2 hours) in just 20 minutes. Continuing training reached 0.874 in 1.8 hours, achieving zero falls across all clips.
sections.details:
### 7.1 Experimental Setup
Evaluations used all 40 clips from the LAFAN1 dataset retargeted to the Unitree G1 (totaling ~2.45 hours of motion), testing whether a single policy could track all clips. The metric is normalized return including fall penalties, matching prior literature. Baselines included the state-of-the-art world model SuperMimic (reported on an H100), PPO running on NablaEngine (under both BeyondMimic and SuperMimic setups), and standard SHAC.

### 7.2 Main Results: Dramatic Acceleration in Wall-Clock Time
Using a single RTX PRO 6000 GPU, $\nabla$Mimic (residual action variant) reached SuperMimic's reported score of 0.82 in just 20 minutes (0.34 hours). Since SuperMimic took 1.2 hours on a more powerful H100, $\nabla$Mimic is roughly $3.5\times$ faster on a cheaper card. Continuing to 1.8 hours reached a score of 0.874, with zero falls across all 40 clips after the 1.5-hour mark in all 3 random seeds.

Alternative gradient sources lagged far behind. Even though PPO stepped $3\times$ faster than usual thanks to NablaEngine, it only reached 0.64 after 3 hours and 0.70 after 6 hours. Piling on cheap samples cannot compete with high-quality gradient information. Furthermore, standard SHAC aborted within 0.06 hours (about 3.5 minutes) due to its gradient explosion guard. Even a modified SHAC with relaxed guards that clipped during explosions only reached 0.816 after 3 hours, failing to hit the 0.82 threshold.

### 7.3 Disentangling Simulator and Algorithm Contributions
Is this dramatic speedup due to NablaEngine's kernel optimizations, or the $\nabla$Mimic algorithm? To separate the two, $\nabla$Mimic was run on MuJoCo Warp's adjoint. Learning curves against update steps matched perfectly between NablaEngine and MuJoCo Warp. This confirms that the high sample efficiency stems strictly from the algorithm, while NablaEngine compresses the wall-clock time per update step by $4.4\times$.

sections.heading: Limitations and future work: Real-robot deployment and generalization
sections.summary: Currently, NablaEngine is specialized for the Unitree G1 on flat ground; expanding to other robots or rough terrain requires custom kernel implementations. Moreover, evaluations remain simulation-bound, leaving real-robot deployment and larger datasets as next milestones.
sections.details:
The authors frankly note several limitations:

- Specialized Robot Model: NablaEngine is finely tuned for Unitree G1 flat-ground locomotion. Adapting it to other robots (such as Boston Dynamics Atlas) or stairs and uneven terrain requires rewriting collision and constraint megakernels.
- No Real-World Experiments: Learned policies have only been evaluated in simulation; zero-shot Sim-to-Real transfer onto physical humanoids remains future work.
- Discrete Contact Switches: Differentiating with fixed contact configurations means smooth gradients across contact mode changes are not strictly captured.
- Bias from Clipping: Truncating extreme outliers via per-sample clipping introduces mathematical bias relative to exact gradients (though practically, this is key to stability).

sections.heading: Summary: A new era for humanoid learning via direct simulator differentiation
sections.summary: By resolving the twin obstacles of extreme outliers and computational cost in exact gradients, this work shows humanoid whole-body control can be learned with ultra-high efficiency directly through simulator derivatives, without world models. Open-sourcing these tools will significantly accelerate future humanoid foundation models.
sections.details:
In contact-rich humanoid control, first-order methods directly differentiating through simulators were long viewed as theoretically promising but practically unusable. This work upends that assumption.

The mathematical issue of gradient spikes was conquered by $\nabla$Mimic's per-sample median-relative clipping and physical action-target regression. The engineering hurdle of heavy computation was cleared by NablaEngine's fused megakernel contact adjoints. Uniting the two enabled a humanoid to master 40 diverse, vigorous human motions on a single GPU in just 20 minutes.

Compressing policy training from days to minutes makes it feasible to train directly on tens of thousands of hours of motion capture data. Open-sourcing $\nabla$Mimic and NablaEngine provides foundational infrastructure to power future humanoid foundation models.

sections.heading: Appendix: Architecture, hyperparameters, and accuracy verification
sections.summary: The policy adopts an encoder-decoder architecture following SuperMimic, facilitating integration with downstream tasks via latent representations. Rigorous comparisons with C MuJoCo confirm high accuracy in both forward and backward passes.
sections.details:
### Encoder-Decoder Architecture
The actor network employs a motion encoder (MLP: 2048-1024-512-256) taking 10 future reference frames to produce a 32-dimensional latent code. A decoder MLP of identical size merges this latent code with past proprioceptive history to output target joint offsets for all 29 joints. Retaining this structure rather than a single monolithic MLP ensures the 32D latent space can be modulated by text instructions or high-level tasks in the future.

### NablaEngine Accuracy Benchmarking
Across 16,384 unseen states, NablaEngine was benchmarked against C MuJoCo (float64, solver tolerance $10^{-13}$). The median velocity error was $8.5 \times 10^{-7}$, and vector-Jacobian product (VJP) gradient errors held a median around $10^{-5}$, closely matching float64 finite differences. Zero divergent or non-finite (NaN/Inf) states were observed.

### Training Hyperparameters
BPTT uses 4,096 parallel environments with a window length of $H=64$ steps. The action-target step size $\delta$ starts at 0.05 radians and follows a cosine decay alongside the learning rate. Multistep regression executes $M=8$ steps with a minibatch size of 2,048 and an Adam learning rate of $3 \times 10^{-4}$.

takeaways: Gradient explosions in contact-rich physics simulators are caused not by the full batch, but by rare singular samples; per-sample median-relative clipping completely neutralizes them.
Rather than using expensive simulator gradients for a single update step, reusing them via multistep regression onto bounded action targets (PODS style) maximizes sample efficiency.
The true value of world-model surrogate gradients lies in outlier suppression and low computational cost; addressing these separately allows exact simulator gradients to outperform world models.
Fusing analytical adjoints into a single GPU megakernel per warp enables full backward passes through contact mechanics in just 0.57 ms—less than half the forward pass time.
limitations: NablaEngine is hand-crafted and specialized for the Unitree G1 on flat ground; applying it to other robots or complex rough terrain requires re-implementing custom kernels.
All evaluations are confined to simulation (LAFAN1 tracking); Sim-to-Real transfer and physical robot durability have not yet been validated.
Clipping extreme outliers on a per-sample basis introduces mathematical bias away from true exact gradients.
